domain: Screen Time — FamilyControls / DeviceActivity / ManagedSettings (+ ManagedSettingsUI), iOS 26.5 shipping, iOS 27 in beta

capabilities.stream: Authorization to use the entire Screen Time stack for yourself (not as a parent)
capabilities.api: AuthorizationCenter.shared.requestAuthorization(for: FamilyControlsMember.individual) async throws; AuthorizationCenter.authorizationStatus -> AuthorizationStatus (.notDetermined/.denied/.approved/.approvedWithDataAccess); revokeAuthorization(completionHandler:)
capabilities.permission: NO Info.plist usage-description key exists for this domain. Runtime consent only: a system sheet + Face ID/Touch ID confirmation of the signed-in Apple Account. Device passcode is MANDATORY (FamilyControlsError.authenticationMethodUnavailable otherwise). Once .individual is approved, re-calls no longer re-prompt.
capabilities.entitlement: com.apple.developer.family-controls (Boolean). REQUIRED. See blockers for the free-Apple-ID gate.
capabilities.notes: .individual is exactly the self-quantified-self case and avoids the parent-Apple-ID/child-account flow entirely. Failure modes are enumerated: FamilyControlsError.authorizationConflict = ANOTHER authorized app already provides parental controls on this device (an existing third-party screen-time app blocks enrollment - uninstall/revoke it first); .invalidAccountType = not signed into iCloud; .networkError = enrollment needs network; .restricted; .unavailable; .authorizationCanceled; .unauthorized (iOS 26.4). Apple explicitly notes that after individual authorization the system REMOVES the restrictions that normally stop a managed user from deleting the authorized app or signing out of iCloud.

capabilities.stream: Per-app foreground time (screen time per app)
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityData.ApplicationActivity.totalActivityDuration: TimeInterval - reachable only from inside a DeviceActivityReportExtension via DeviceActivityReportScene configuration -> DeviceActivityResults<DeviceActivityData>
capabilities.permission: none beyond the FamilyControls authorization above
capabilities.backfill: Up to ~1 month, but per an Apple Frameworks Engineer: 'Once your app has successfully received authorization using FamilyControls, your DeviceActivityReportExtension will have access to up to a month of device activity data FROM THAT DATE ONWARD.' Read conservatively: assume ~0 retrospective backfill on day 1 and a rolling ~30-day window thereafter. Community reports of pre-authorization data appearing are inconsistent - contested.
capabilities.resolution: DeviceActivityFilter.SegmentInterval.hourly(during:) / .daily(during:) / .weekly(during:). Hourly is the finest documented segmentation.
capabilities.notes: RENDER-ONLY. This number can be drawn on screen and cannot be extracted - see the sandbox row. This is the single most important asymmetry in the whole domain.

capabilities.stream: Per-app pickups (times the device was picked up directly into that app)
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityData.ApplicationActivity.numberOfPickups: Int
capabilities.notes: Render-only inside the report extension.

capabilities.stream: Per-app notification count
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityData.ApplicationActivity.numberOfNotifications: Int
capabilities.notes: This is otherwise UNOBTAINABLE on iOS - UNUserNotificationCenter only exposes YOUR app's notifications. Render-only.

capabilities.stream: App identity attached to activity rows
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityData.ApplicationActivity.application: Application; Application.token: ApplicationToken?; Application.bundleIdentifier: String?; Application.localizedDisplayName: String?
capabilities.notes: CONTESTED / important. Apple's docs state bundleIdentifier and localizedDisplayName are populated ONLY 'in an extension that provides shield configurations' and are nil elsewhere. A widely-cited claim that they are also populated inside a DeviceActivityReportExtension is asserted in forum posts and blogs but is NOT in Apple's documentation, and a long-running forum thread (709692, 'ApplicationActivity.application.localizedDisplayName always nil') reports it nil there. Treat token->name resolution inside the report extension as unreliable; use SwiftUI Label(token) instead.

capabilities.stream: Per-category time (Social, Games, Productivity, etc.)
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityData.CategoryActivity.totalActivityDuration: TimeInterval; .category: ActivityCategory; .applications: DeviceActivityResults<ApplicationActivity>; .webDomains: DeviceActivityResults<WebDomainActivity>
capabilities.notes: Categories are Apple's own App Store taxonomy; the set is not enumerable pre-26.4 (see FamilyActivityData.activityCategories).

capabilities.stream: Per-web-domain browsing time
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityData.WebDomainActivity.totalActivityDuration: TimeInterval; .webDomain: WebDomain (WebDomain.domain: String? - nil outside shield-config extensions)
capabilities.backfill: ~30-day rolling; the domains offered in FamilyActivityPicker are themselves sourced from the last 30 days of WebKit usage
capabilities.notes: Safari/WebKit-sourced. Known data-quality complaints in 26.x: forum reports of single domains showing 20h/day and hundreds of hours/week - sanity-check any web-domain series before believing it.

capabilities.stream: Total device screen time per time segment
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityData.ActivitySegment.totalActivityDuration: TimeInterval; .dateInterval: DateInterval; DeviceActivityData.activitySegments: DeviceActivityResults<ActivitySegment>
capabilities.notes: This is the headline 'Screen Time' number from Settings.

capabilities.stream: First device pickup of the day/segment
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityData.ActivitySegment.firstPickup: Date?
capabilities.notes: Excellent wake-time proxy - the closest thing iOS gives to 'when did you actually get up'. Render-only.

capabilities.stream: Longest single continuous usage session in a segment
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityData.ActivitySegment.longestActivity: DateInterval?
capabilities.notes: Binge/doomscroll detector. Render-only.

capabilities.stream: Pickups that did NOT lead to any app use (glance-only unlocks)
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityData.ActivitySegment.totalPickupsWithoutApplicationActivity: Int
capabilities.notes: Compulsive-checking metric; not surfaced anywhere in the Settings UI.

capabilities.stream: Which physical device the activity came from (iPhone vs iPad vs Mac vs iPod), and its user-set name
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityData.device: DeviceActivityData.Device; Device.model: Device.Model (.iPhone/.iPad/.mac/.iPod); Device.name: String?; filter via DeviceActivityFilter.Devices.all
capabilities.permission: none beyond FamilyControls authorization; requires Screen Time 'Share Across Devices' to be ON for cross-device rollup
capabilities.notes: DIRECTLY RELEVANT TO A 4-DEVICE SETUP. DeviceActivityFilter.Devices.all = 'all devices that are sharing activity data with the current device', and DeviceActivityAuthorization.sharingEnabled (iOS 17+) reports whether sharing is on. So one app on the iPhone can report iPad usage too. Note the Model enum has NO watch case - Apple Watch usage is not in this dataset at all.

capabilities.stream: Identity of the person the data belongs to
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityData.user: DeviceActivityData.User; User.appleID: String?; User.nameComponents: PersonNameComponents?; User.role: User.FamilyRole (.individual / .child); filter via DeviceActivityFilter.Users.all / .children
capabilities.notes: For self-monitoring, role will be .individual. Render-only like everything else in the report extension.

capabilities.stream: Freshness of the underlying dataset
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityData.lastUpdatedDate: Date; DeviceActivityData.segmentInterval: DeviceActivityFilter.SegmentInterval
capabilities.notes: The system's own admission that the data is cached and lags. Pair with DeviceActivityData.Policy.live (26.4) whose doc explicitly warns 'A request to fetch live data may return cached data if the system updated the cache recently.'

capabilities.stream: THE PRIVACY SANDBOX ITSELF - what can be rendered vs. what can be extracted
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityReport(_:filter:) SwiftUI view; DeviceActivityReportExtension : AppExtension; DeviceActivityReportScene; DeviceActivityReportBuilder; DeviceActivityReport.Context; extension point identifier com.apple.deviceactivityui.report-extension
capabilities.entitlement: com.apple.developer.family-controls (request separately for the extension's bundle ID for distribution)
capabilities.notes: CONFIRMED, APPLE'S OWN WORDS: 'To protect the user's privacy, your extension runs in a sandbox. This sandbox prevents your extension from making network requests or moving sensitive content outside the extension's address space.' Empirically corroborated: App Group UserDefaults writes, App Group file writes, Core Data writes, NotificationCenter and Darwin notifications ALL fail from this extension; developers report the report extension gets its own private UserDefaults store even when using the same suiteName. Data flows IN only (host app can seed config via App Group; the host passes a DeviceActivityFilter into the view). RENDERABLE: any SwiftUI view - numbers, charts, text, Labels. EXTRACTABLE: nothing. Not even one integer. The host app receives an opaque rendered view, never the values. Practical corollary: you can build a beautiful in-app dashboard you cannot export, back up, or compute on. NOTE the same sandbox sentence appears verbatim on ShieldConfigurationDataSource - the 'leak app names via the shield extension' idea is officially blocked by the same wording, though community reports of App Group writes succeeding from shield extensions exist and are contested.

capabilities.stream: Per-app / per-category usage RECONSTRUCTED as extractable numbers (the threshold-counting technique)
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityCenter.startMonitoring(_ activity: DeviceActivityName, during schedule: DeviceActivitySchedule, events: [DeviceActivityEvent.Name : DeviceActivityEvent]) throws; DeviceActivityEvent(applications:categories:webDomains:threshold:includesPastActivity:); DeviceActivityMonitor.eventDidReachThreshold(_:activity:); DeviceActivityCenter.stopMonitoring(_:), .activities, .events(for:), .schedule(for:)
capabilities.entitlement: com.apple.developer.family-controls (app AND the DeviceActivityMonitor extension bundle ID)
capabilities.backfill: none - forward only from startMonitoring. Apple: 'the system will only consider the person's device activity when it starts monitoring the event.' DeviceActivityEvent.includesPastActivity (iOS 17.4+) only reaches back to the start of the CURRENT interval (and rounds to the nearest whole hour), not to before installation.
capabilities.resolution: threshold is a DateComponents - minute-level is expressible and used in practice. Best documented working recipe: 12 two-hour schedules covering 00:00-24:00, each with 24 events at 5-minute increments (5,10,...,120 min) => ~5-minute resolution across the whole day, at the cost of ~12 of your ~20 activity budget. 1-minute events are expressible but multiply event count past what the system tolerates and worsen the reliability problems below.
capabilities.notes: THIS IS THE ONLY WAY TO GET SCREEN-TIME NUMBERS OUT AS DATA pre-26.4. You count callbacks. LIMITS: max 20 activities monitored at once by the app + its extensions (community/undocumented number; Apple documents only the error case DeviceActivityCenter.MonitoringError.excessiveActivities). Schedule interval min 15 minutes / max 1 week (community/undocumented; Apple documents only .intervalTooShort / .intervalTooLong / .invalidDateComponents). Events-per-activity limit is UNDOCUMENTED with no Apple statement - the one forum thread asking directly (681955) has zero replies after 5 years. YES it needs an App Group: the monitor extension is a separate process and must write counters to a shared App Group UserDefaults/file for the host app to read. It DOES survive reboot - schedules are system-persisted and re-fire, and App Group UserDefaults is on-disk; but in-memory extension state is not, so every callback must write through immediately. RELIABILITY IS THE REAL PROBLEM: an Apple Frameworks Engineer acknowledged (Nov 2024) an unresolved bug where thresholds fire in a bunch (1h/2h/3h notifications arriving together) because the extension was terminated and iOS 17+ retries queued events; developers report the extension being killed after a few days; hard memory ceiling ~5-6 MB with Jetsam kills; and open 26.x forum threads report intervalDidStart never firing at all on 26.3.1. Budget for lossy counting, not exact accounting.

capabilities.stream: Device-in-use / session boundary signals
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityMonitor.intervalDidStart(for:), .intervalDidEnd(for:), .intervalWillStartWarning(for:), .intervalWillEndWarning(for:), .eventWillReachThresholdWarning(_:activity:); DeviceActivitySchedule(intervalStart:intervalEnd:repeats:warningTime:), .nextInterval
capabilities.resolution: schedule-boundary granularity (min 15-min interval, community); warningTime is a DateComponents and 1 minute is used in practice
capabilities.notes: NON-OBVIOUS AND USEFUL: Apple documents that intervalDidStart fires when someone FIRST USES THE DEVICE within the interval - 'the system only invokes this method when the device is in use'. Same for intervalDidEnd. So a chain of short repeating schedules gives you a coarse device-active/idle timeline for free, independent of any app selection, with no threshold math. This is the cheapest reliable signal in the whole framework.

capabilities.stream: iOS 26.4: real per-app usage fetched IN-PROCESS and exportable (no report-extension sandbox)
capabilities.api: static func DeviceActivityData.activityData(filteredBy filter: DeviceActivityFilter = .init(), using policy: DeviceActivityData.Policy = .cached) -> some AsyncSequence<DeviceActivityData, any Error>; DeviceActivityData.Policy.cached / .live; DeviceActivityData.Error.missingData / .unauthorized / .unavailable
capabilities.permission: AuthorizationStatus must be .approvedWithDataAccess - a strictly higher consent tier than .approved. Forum report (thread 820283, Mar 2026, unanswered): once the app declares the capability, users get an all-or-nothing choice - there is no way to grant shielding without also granting usage-data access.
capabilities.entitlement: com.apple.developer.family-controls.app-and-website-usage - a SECOND, SEPARATE entitlement on top of com.apple.developer.family-controls. Apple: 'Adding the Family Controls capability to your app automatically sets this entitlement. However, before submitting your app to the App Store, you must request permission to use the entitlement.'
capabilities.backfill: Governed by the same DeviceActivityFilter as the report path, so expect the same ~30-day rolling ceiling. Apple has published no separate backfill figure for this API.
capabilities.resolution: Same DeviceActivityFilter.SegmentInterval hourly/daily/weekly, same full DeviceActivityData tree (ApplicationActivity, CategoryActivity, WebDomainActivity, ActivitySegment)
capabilities.notes: THE HEADLINE CHANGE AND THE WHOLE BALLGAME - it converts the domain from 'render-only' to 'real exportable quantified-self data'. Apple's own framing: 'Use this method to export family activity data, for use in another app or platform.' It is an async sequence callable from the HOST APP, so no sandbox; not itself a background wake source, but pair it with DeviceActivityMonitor callbacks or BGTaskScheduler to pull on a schedule. BUT THE REGION GATE IS UNRESOLVED AND MUST NOT BE ASSUMED FAVOURABLE. Apple's exact wording, repeated verbatim on both this method and on FamilyActivityData: 'You can develop and test an app that uses this method on devices in any region. Customer installations of your app can only use the method on devices located in the EU that are signed in with an Apple Account with an EU country or region. Otherwise, it throws an error.' TWO READINGS: (a) the discriminator is the provisioning-profile/installation type, so a development-signed sideloaded build is 'develop and test' and works on a US device - the first sentence points this way; (b) the discriminator is the runtime device region + Apple Account country, in which case a Dallas iPhone with a US Apple Account throws regardless of signing - the second sentence describes that as the actual enforcement mechanism. Apple does not say which check fires. Verify empirically on-device before designing around it. FALLBACK IF IT BITES: the whole 26.4 path collapses back to pre-26.4 reality - opaque tokens, report-extension sandbox, threshold reconstruction.

capabilities.stream: iOS 26.4: the installed-app inventory WITH real bundle identifiers (token de-anonymisation)
capabilities.api: FamilyActivityData.shared.installedApplications: [Application] { get async throws } - 'Each application contains both a bundleIdentifier and a token.'
capabilities.backfill: none - current inventory snapshot, not historical
capabilities.notes: This is the answer to 'can you resolve an ApplicationToken to an app name?' - PRE-26.4: NO. POST-26.4 WITH THE NEW ENTITLEMENT: YES, and better than yes - it hands you the bundleIdentifier<->token mapping for every installed app, which you can then join against every ApplicationToken you hold. It also gives you an app-inventory stream that has never before been available to a third-party iOS app at all. Async property on the host app, so no sandbox. Same EU/region caveat as the row above.

capabilities.stream: iOS 26.4: visited web domains as real domain strings
capabilities.api: FamilyActivityData.shared.visitedWebDomains: [WebDomain] { get async throws } - 'Each web domain contains both a domain and a token.'
capabilities.backfill: WebKit-sourced; the picker's equivalent list is last-30-days
capabilities.notes: Domain strings, not opaque tokens - join to WebDomainActivity.totalActivityDuration for a named browsing-time series. Same EU/region caveat.

capabilities.stream: iOS 26.4: the full category taxonomy with display names
capabilities.api: FamilyActivityData.shared.activityCategories: Set<ActivityCategory> { get async throws } - 'Each category contains both a localizedDisplayName and a token.'
capabilities.notes: 'The set of ALL POSSIBLE activity categories' - previously there was no way to enumerate Apple's category list at all; you could only receive opaque ActivityCategoryTokens from the picker. Same EU/region caveat.

capabilities.stream: User's own selection of which apps/categories/domains to track
capabilities.api: FamilyActivityPicker(headerText:footerText:selection:) SwiftUI view; FamilyActivitySelection (applicationTokens: Set<ApplicationToken>, categoryTokens: Set<ActivityCategoryToken>, webDomainTokens: Set<WebDomainToken>, applications: Set<Application>, categories: Set<ActivityCategory>, webDomains: Set<WebDomain>, includeEntireCategory: Bool)
capabilities.permission: none beyond FamilyControls authorization - the picker is a system view; your app never sees the choices in cleartext (pre-26.4)
capabilities.notes: Requires user interaction, so never background. THE PICKER IS THE ONLY SOURCE OF ApplicationTokens - Apple confirms tokens cannot be minted from a bundle ID (Application(bundleIdentifier:) produces an Application whose .token is nil). So the app cannot programmatically decide to track 'all apps'; the human must tap through the system picker once. Selecting a whole category returns only the category token, not the member app tokens. FamilyActivitySelection is Codable, so persist it in the App Group so the monitor extension can read it.

capabilities.stream: Showing an app's real name and icon on screen without ever learning them
capabilities.api: Label(_: ApplicationToken) / Label(_: ActivityCategoryToken) / Label(_: WebDomainToken); FamilyActivityIconView; FamilyActivityTitleView; ManagedSettings.Token<T> (ApplicationToken = Token<Application>, WebDomainToken = Token<WebDomain>, ActivityCategoryToken = Token<ActivityCategory>)
capabilities.notes: THE TOKEN OPACITY ANSWER (pre-26.4): a Token is, in Apple's words, 'A representation of an activity, such as an app or website, that doesn't reveal its identity.' You can RENDER it - Label(token) paints the real name and icon - but you cannot READ it. There is no token->String API, no reflection path Apple supports, and Application.bundleIdentifier is nil everywhere except a shield-configuration extension. So a pre-26.4 app can show the user a perfectly labelled chart of their own apps while being structurally incapable of knowing which apps they are.

capabilities.stream: App/category/domain NAMES exposed to a shield-configuration extension
capabilities.api: ShieldConfigurationDataSource.configuration(shielding: Application) / (shielding: WebDomain) / (shielding: Application, in: ActivityCategory) / (shielding: WebDomain, in: ActivityCategory) -> ShieldConfiguration; ShieldConfiguration(backgroundBlurStyle:backgroundColor:icon:title:subtitle:primaryButtonLabel:primaryButtonBackgroundColor:secondaryButtonLabel:secondaryButtonSubmenuItems:); ShieldConfiguration.Label(text:color:)
capabilities.entitlement: com.apple.developer.family-controls (request for the extension bundle ID too)
capabilities.notes: Fires only when a shielded app is launched, so it is event-driven rather than schedulable. Apple: 'The system provides your extension with the display names, bundle identifiers, and domains for each application, website, or category it shields.' This is the one place cleartext identity is handed over pre-26.4 - WHICH IS WHY APPLE PUT THE SAME SANDBOX ON IT: 'your extension runs in a sandbox. This sandbox prevents your extension from making network requests or moving sensitive content outside the extension's address space.' Community reports that App Group writes from this extension DO succeed exist and are CONTESTED against Apple's stated restriction; if it works it is undocumented behaviour that can be closed at any point. Do not architect a personal app on it now that 26.4 gives a sanctioned path.

capabilities.stream: User taps on a block screen (self-reported intent events)
capabilities.api: ShieldActionDelegate.handle(action: ShieldAction, for: ApplicationToken | WebDomainToken | ActivityCategoryToken, completionHandler: (ShieldActionResponse) -> Void); ShieldAction .primaryButtonPressed / .secondaryButtonPressed / .firstSecondarySubmenuItemPressed / .secondSecondarySubmenuItemPressed / .thirdSecondarySubmenuItemPressed; ShieldActionResponse .none / .close / .defer / .openParentalControlsApp
capabilities.notes: Runs on shield interaction without the host app being open. A genuinely underused telemetry channel: every time you hit your own block screen and choose 'give me 5 more minutes', that is a labelled relapse event with a timestamp and a token. Apple states this extension is given only TOKENS, not names - unlike the shield-CONFIGURATION extension. Apple documents no sandbox on ShieldActionDelegate, so App Group writes are the normal path here. The iOS 26.4 submenu items let you offer three distinct 'why' buttons - i.e. self-reported reason codes.

capabilities.stream: Applying and enumerating restrictions (the write side, plus a small readable surface)
capabilities.api: ManagedSettingsStore(named: ManagedSettingsStore.Name); .shield (ShieldSettings.applications: Set<ApplicationToken>?, .webDomains, .applicationCategories/.webDomainCategories: ShieldSettings.ActivityCategoryPolicy<T> = .none/.all(except:)/.specific(_:except:)); .application (blockedApplications, denyAppInstallation, denyAppRemoval); .appStore (denyInAppPurchases, maximumRating, requirePasswordForPurchases); .media (denyExplicitContent, denyBookstoreErotica, denyMusicService, maximumMovieRating, maximumTVShowRating); .webContent (blockedByFilter: FilterPolicy .none/.all(except:)/.auto(_:except:)/.specific(_:)); .safari (cookiePolicy: .always/.currentWebsite/.never/.visitedWebsites, denyAutoFill); .siri (denySiri); .gameCenter (denyAddingFriends, denyMultiplayerGaming); .account (lockAccounts); .cellular (lockAppCellularData, lockCellularPlan, lockESIM); .dateAndTime (requireAutomaticDateAndTime); .passcode (lockPasscode); clearAllSettings(); READABLE: effectiveMaximumMovieRating, effectiveMaximumTVShowRating, effectiveDenyExplicitContent (+ $-prefixed Combine publishers)
capabilities.notes: The monitor extension holds a ManagedSettingsStore and applies shields from its callbacks, hence background-capable. That is the COMPLETE ManagedSettings surface - 13 setting groups, every property listed. Note it is almost entirely WRITE-ONLY: the only readable-back values are the three effective* content-rating properties. LIMITS: 50 named stores per process (WWDC22); ~50 tokens per shield setting and it FAILS SILENTLY - no error thrown, the store simply shields nothing and the property reads back nil. iOS 26.5 additions are materially useful: ManagedSettingsStore.stores enumerates your own stores, isActive toggles a store out of the effective calculation without destroying it, deleteStore()/deleteStores(_:) clean up.

capabilities.stream: Token expiry / re-validation (iOS 26.5)
capabilities.api: ManagedSettingsStore.TokenExpiryMessage (posted on NotificationCenter); static func ManagedSettingsStore.refresh(_ tokens: inout [ApplicationToken]) throws; refresh(_ tokens: inout [ActivityCategoryToken]) throws; refresh(_ tokens: inout [WebDomainToken]) throws
capabilities.notes: Apple's docs: 'A message that is posted in NotificationCenter when ManagedSettingsStore tokens are expired... Use these messages to refresh tokens in your database that are expired.' Apple has now formally admitted the thing developers hit for years: TOKENS GO STALE. Before 26.5 the only fix reported in the forums was telling the user to unselect and reselect every app in the picker to mint fresh tokens. See blockers - this is a longitudinal-data-integrity problem, not just an API detail.

capabilities.stream: Cross-device activity sharing state (iPhone + iPad rollup)
capabilities.api: DeviceActivityAuthorization.sharingEnabled: Bool { get }; .authorizedClientIdentifiers: [String]; .isOverridden: Bool { get set }; DeviceActivityAuthorizing.isAuthorized: Bool; DeviceActivityAuthorizing.isAuthorized(_ bundleIdentifier: String) -> Bool
capabilities.notes: Entirely undocumented by Apple (empty abstracts) but present and public. sharingEnabled is the programmatic read of Screen Time's 'Share Across Devices' switch, which is the precondition for DeviceActivityFilter.Devices.all returning iPad data to an iPhone app. isAuthorized(bundleIdentifier:) lets you check whether a SPECIFIC other app holds Family Controls authorization - the practical way to diagnose FamilyControlsError.authorizationConflict.

capabilities.stream: ALTERNATIVE: per-app open/close timestamps with no entitlement at all (Shortcuts personal automation)
capabilities.framework: Shortcuts (app, not an SDK) + App Intents for the payload
capabilities.api: Shortcuts > Automation > New Automation > App > [pick app] > 'Is Opened' / 'Is Closed' > Run Immediately (turn OFF 'Notify When Run'). Action body can call an AppIntent you expose from your own app (AppIntent / AppEntity), or Append to Text File / Get Current Date.
capabilities.permission: none - no entitlement, no Info.plist key, no Screen Time authorization. Runs on a FREE Apple ID.
capabilities.backfill: none - forward only from the moment you create each automation
capabilities.resolution: exact open and close timestamps per app; duration = close minus open
capabilities.minIOS: iOS 13+ for app triggers; 'Run Immediately' (no confirmation prompt) since iOS 15
capabilities.notes: THE ONLY PER-APP USAGE PATH THAT WORKS ON A FREE APPLE ID, and it produces something the Screen Time API never does: exact session boundaries rather than aggregated buckets. The automation fires without the user being in your app, hence background-capable. THE COSTS ARE REAL. (1) There is NO API to create automations - no App Intents, no MDM profile, no URL scheme. You hand-build TWO automations per app in the Shortcuts UI. Thirty apps = sixty automations, tapped in by hand. (2) 'Is Closed' is widely reported as the less reliable of the pair - backgrounding vs. swiping away vs. being jetsammed do not all fire it, so sessions can be left open and must be closed heuristically. (3) It cannot see apps you did not pre-enumerate, cannot see pickups, notifications, or web domains, and cannot see the iPad from the iPhone. Verdict: awkward and manual, not impossible - and the correct answer for anyone unwilling to pay $99/yr.

blockers: FREE APPLE ID: FAMILY CONTROLS IS FLATLY IMPOSSIBLE. This is the decisive fact and it is settled by Apple's own capability matrix, not by inference. On 'Supported capabilities (iOS)' (https://developer.apple.com/help/account/reference/supported-capabilities-ios/) the row 'Family Controls (development) *' is checked for ADP (paid Apple Developer Program, $99/yr) and UNCHECKED for both ADEP (Enterprise) and 'Apple Developer' - the latter being Apple's own label for the free tier ('Apple Account holders who have agreed to the Apple Developer Agreement... No cost is associated with this agreement and developers can't distribute apps'), i.e. the Xcode Personal Team. You cannot enable the capability, cannot get a provisioning profile carrying com.apple.developer.family-controls, and the build will not sign. No AltStore/SideStore workaround exists - those re-sign with the SAME free personal certificate and inherit the same entitlement whitelist. There is no jailbreak-free bypass. The $99/yr Apple Developer Program is a hard prerequisite for this entire domain. (Note: App Groups is NOT a second gate - the same table shows 'App groups' checked for the free tier, contradicting several blog posts that claim otherwise. One gate, not two.)

NOTHING - NOT ONE BYTE - CAN LEAVE A DeviceActivityReportExtension. Apple: 'To protect the user's privacy, your extension runs in a sandbox. This sandbox prevents your extension from making network requests or moving sensitive content outside the extension's address space.' Independently confirmed empirically: App Group UserDefaults writes, App Group file writes, Core Data, NotificationCenter and Darwin notifications all fail; the extension is even reported to get a private UserDefaults store despite an identical suiteName. There is no supported way to return a single integer to the host app. Every rich number in DeviceActivityData - per-app duration, pickups, notifications, firstPickup, longestActivity - is viewable and non-extractable through this path. Pre-26.4 this is the defining constraint of the domain and it is genuinely impossible, not merely awkward.

NO RETROSPECTIVE BACKFILL WORTH THE NAME. Per an Apple Frameworks Engineer, the report extension gets 'up to a month of device activity data from that date onward' - i.e. the clock starts at authorization. The monitor/threshold path is strictly forward-only: Apple states 'the system will only consider the person's device activity when it starts monitoring the event', and includesPastActivity (iOS 17.4) reaches back only to the start of the current interval, rounded to the nearest whole hour. Practically: install the app today and you have a dashboard with nothing in it. There is no way to import your existing Screen Time history.

knowledgeC.db / Biome / RMAdminStore ARE NOT IN A LOCAL BACKUP. The forensics path is real but it is a FULL-FILESYSTEM path, not a backup path. Multiple current forensics sources state that knowledgeC.db, the Biome databases, netusage.sqlite and 'detailed Screen Time data' (RMAdminStore-Local.sqlite / RMAdminStore-Cloud.sqlite at /private/var/mobile/Library/Application Support/com.apple.remotemanagementd/) all require full filesystem acquisition - which on a modern, patched, non-jailbroken iPhone means a hardware exploit (checkm8-class, A11 and earlier) or a commercial tool like GrayKey/Cellebrite. An encrypted Finder/iTunes backup does NOT contain these domains, and encrypting the backup does not change which domains are backed up - it changes which of the backed-up domains include secrets. Compounding it: knowledgeC has been progressively superseded by Biome since iOS 16, and Biome stores are proprietary 'SEGB' files, not SQLite, so even with the bytes your existing tooling does not read them. The macOS equivalent (~/Library/Application Support/Knowledge/knowledgeC.db, readable with Full Disk Access via APOLLO/ScreenTime2CSV) works fine - but it gives you Mac data, not iPhone data. VERDICT: impossible on the phone without jailbreaking it.

APPLICATION TOKENS ARE NOT A STABLE PRIMARY KEY - THIS BREAKS LONGITUDINAL DATA. iOS 26.5 shipped ManagedSettingsStore.TokenExpiryMessage and three refresh(_:) overloads precisely because tokens expire; before that, the only remedy reported in the forums after an iOS update invalidated tokens was to make the user unselect and reselect every app in the FamilyActivityPicker to mint new ones. For a quantified-self app whose entire value is a multi-month per-app time series, this is a first-order threat: your historical rows are keyed on an identifier that can silently stop joining to the app it came from. Mitigations: subscribe to TokenExpiryMessage and call refresh() (26.5+); or, if the iOS 26.4 data-access entitlement is available to you, key your series on the real bundleIdentifier from FamilyActivityData.installedApplications and treat tokens as ephemeral lookup handles. There is no pre-26.4, pre-26.5 mitigation other than re-picking.

THE iOS 26.4 EXPORT PATH MAY BE EU-ONLY AT RUNTIME - UNRESOLVED, DO NOT ASSUME IT WORKS IN TEXAS. Apple's wording, identical on both DeviceActivityData.activityData(filteredBy:using:) and FamilyActivityData: 'You can develop and test an app that uses this method on devices in any region. Customer installations of your app can only use the method on devices located in the EU that are signed in with an Apple Account with an EU country or region. Otherwise, it throws an error.' Sentence one suggests the discriminator is installation/profile type, which would make a development-signed sideloaded personal build work anywhere. Sentence two describes the actual enforcement as device region + Apple Account country, which would fail on a US device regardless of signing. Apple does not say which check fires, and I found no developer report resolving it. This must be tested on-device before any architecture depends on it. If it bites, everything gained in 26.4 - exportable data, bundleIdentifier resolution, the installed-app inventory - is unavailable, and you are back to opaque tokens, the report-extension sandbox, and threshold reconstruction.

THERE IS NO 'READ SCREEN TIME' API FOR NON-FAMILY-CONTROLS APPS. Focus filters (AppIntents / SetFocusFilterIntent) expose which Focus is active and let your app react to it - they expose NOTHING about which apps the user is in or for how long. App Intents likewise: they let OTHER things invoke YOUR app; they give you no visibility into other apps. Neither is an alternative source of usage data. Similarly there is no per-app usage in UIDevice, ProcessInfo, CoreMotion, or any public analytics API. Anyone claiming otherwise is describing either the Screen Time API or a Shortcuts automation.

YOU CANNOT PROGRAMMATICALLY CHOOSE WHAT TO TRACK. ApplicationTokens can only be minted by the user tapping through the system FamilyActivityPicker - Application(bundleIdentifier:) yields an Application whose .token is nil, and Apple confirms tokens are not generated from bundle IDs. So 'track everything automatically' is not expressible; a human must sit down once and select apps. Selecting a whole category returns only the category token, not its member app tokens, so per-app resolution inside a category still requires enumerating the apps by hand. (iOS 26.4's FamilyActivityData.installedApplications gives you the inventory but does not substitute for the picker's role in minting selection tokens.)

THE MONITOR EXTENSION IS UNRELIABLE ENOUGH TO CORRUPT YOUR DATA, AND APPLE HAS ACKNOWLEDGED IT. An Apple Frameworks Engineer responded in Nov 2024 to a report that thresholds fire in bunches - 1h, 2h and 3h callbacks arriving simultaneously because the extension was terminated and iOS 17+ queues failed events for retry - with 'Our engineering teams need to investigate this issue, as resolution may involve changes to Apple's software.' Add: a hard ~5-6 MB memory ceiling with Jetsam kills, reports of the extension being killed after a few days of running, and open iOS 26.x threads reporting intervalDidStart never firing at all on 26.3.1 and the report extension process never launching on 26.4. If you count callbacks to reconstruct usage, you must design for lost, late and duplicated events - idempotent keys per (activity, event, interval), not a naive counter.

KEY LIMITS ARE UNDOCUMENTED, AND ONE FAILS SILENTLY. Apple documents the ERROR (DeviceActivityCenter.MonitoringError.excessiveActivities / .intervalTooShort / .intervalTooLong / .invalidDateComponents / .unauthorized) but never the NUMBER. The widely-repeated figures - 20 simultaneous activities per app+extensions, 15-minute minimum and 1-week maximum schedule interval - are community-derived, and the direct forum question asking Apple for them (thread 681955, Jun 2021) still has zero replies. The per-activity EVENT count limit has no published figure from any source, community included. Worst of all, the ~50-token shield limit throws NOTHING: exceed it and the store silently shields nothing and reads back nil. Discover your real ceilings empirically on-device and handle throws around every startMonitoring call.
nonObvious: THE 20-ACTIVITY BUDGET IS THE REAL DESIGN CONSTRAINT, AND THE KNOWN-GOOD RECIPE IS 12x24. The published working technique (matteing.com) spends the budget like this: 12 schedules of two hours each tile the full 24-hour day, and EACH carries 24 DeviceActivityEvents with thresholds at 5, 10, 15 ... 120 minutes. Every callback you receive is worth 5 minutes of usage; you count them. That yields ~5-minute resolution across an entire day while consuming only 12 of the ~20 activities, leaving headroom for a shield schedule. Going to 1-minute thresholds is expressible in DateComponents but multiplies events per activity past what the system tolerates and makes the retry-bunching bug far worse. A competent developer's first instinct - one activity per app - burns the budget at 20 apps and gives no time resolution at all.

intervalDidStart FIRES ONLY WHEN THE DEVICE IS ACTUALLY IN USE - THAT IS A FREE IDLE/ACTIVE TIMELINE. Apple states it plainly on both intervalDidStart(for:) and intervalDidEnd(for:): 'the system only invokes this method when the device is in use.' So a chain of short repeating DeviceActivitySchedules gives you a coarse device-active timeline with zero threshold arithmetic, zero app selection, and no dependence on the flaky threshold-retry machinery. Almost nobody uses this; everyone reaches straight for eventDidReachThreshold. Combine it with DeviceActivitySchedule.warningTime (a DateComponents - 1 minute works) and intervalWillEndWarning for a pre-roll signal.

THE FOUR EXTENSIONS HAVE FOUR DIFFERENT SANDBOXES, AND CONFLATING THEM IS THE MOST COMMON ERROR IN THIS DOMAIN. DeviceActivityReportExtension: Apple explicitly sandboxes it - no network, nothing leaves the address space (this is the one that cannot write to an App Group). ShieldConfigurationDataSource: Apple applies the SAME sandbox sentence, but uniquely the system hands it real display names, bundle identifiers and domains. ShieldActionDelegate: Apple documents NO sandbox, but the system gives it only tokens, never names. DeviceActivityMonitor: Apple documents NO sandbox at all - and App Group writes from it are the standard, working mechanism every screen-time app on the App Store relies on. Search results and blog posts routinely blur these into one 'the Screen Time extensions are sandboxed' claim; that claim is wrong for the monitor extension and it matters enormously, because the monitor extension is your ONLY data exfiltration route pre-26.4. Separately contested: NETWORK from the monitor extension - matteing reports successfully posting usage to a remote server, while forum thread 724649 reports requests rarely arriving even with URLSessionConfiguration.sharedContainerIdentifier set and performExpiringActivity wrapping. For a local personal app this is moot - write to the App Group and let the host app upload.

THE DEVELOPMENT ENTITLEMENT IS SELF-SERVE ONCE YOU PAY THE $99; ONLY DISTRIBUTION IS APPROVAL-GATED. Apple's 'Configuring Family Controls' states it directly: 'Xcode automatically updates your app target's entitlements file to include the com.apple.developer.family-controls entitlement key set to true, AND YOU CAN ACCESS THE ENTITLEMENT THROUGH THE APPLE DEVELOPER PROGRAM DURING DEVELOPMENT.' Tick the capability, let automatic signing regenerate the profile, build to your own device - no form, no wait, no review. The approval-gated request at developer.apple.com/contact/request/family-controls-distribution is required only to ship (TestFlight/Ad Hoc/App Store), and it must be filed SEPARATELY FOR EVERY EXTENSION BUNDLE ID (Device Activity Monitor, Device Activity Report, Shield Action, Shield Configuration) as well as the app. Apple grants it as a 'managed capability' and the status shows as 'Assigned' in Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles. Reported turnaround spans ~1 business day to ~4.5 weeks, median a few business days to a couple of weeks; the form is login-gated (it 302s to idmsa.apple.com) so its exact fields are not publicly verifiable, but developers report it asks for the app/bundle ID, a description of the parental-control or digital-wellbeing use case, and a website URL (a GitHub page has been accepted). For a personal sideloaded app NONE OF THIS APPLIES - you never need the distribution entitlement. The gate is the $99, not Apple's review.

iOS 26.4 QUIETLY DEMOLISHED THE CENTRAL PRIVACY WALL - AND ALMOST NOBODY HAS NOTICED. com.apple.developer.family-controls.app-and-website-usage plus AuthorizationStatus.approvedWithDataAccess unlocks FamilyActivityData.installedApplications, which per Apple's own text yields Applications carrying 'both a bundleIdentifier and a token'. That single sentence ends four years of token opacity: you can now join every ApplicationToken you hold to a real bundle ID. Pair it with DeviceActivityData.activityData(filteredBy:using:) - an in-process AsyncSequence that Apple says exists to 'export family activity data, for use in another app or platform' - and the entire report-extension sandbox becomes optional rather than mandatory. This is almost certainly a Digital Markets Act response, which is why the runtime is region-fenced. If you are building this domain in mid-2026, THIS is the API to design around, with the pre-26.4 threshold machinery as the fallback - not the other way round. Caveat from the field (forum 820283, unanswered): declaring the capability appears to make consent all-or-nothing, with no way for the user to grant shielding without also granting usage-data access.

ONE APP ON THE iPHONE CAN REPORT THE iPAD. DeviceActivityFilter.Devices.all is documented as filtering 'data for ALL DEVICES THAT ARE SHARING ACTIVITY DATA WITH THE CURRENT DEVICE', DeviceActivityData.Device.model distinguishes .iPhone/.iPad/.mac/.iPod, and DeviceActivityAuthorization.sharingEnabled (iOS 17+, undocumented but public) is the programmatic read of Screen Time's 'Share Across Devices' toggle. So you build and sign ONE iPhone app and get iPad usage for free - provided the toggle is on. The corollary matters just as much: Device.Model has NO watch case. Apple Watch usage does not exist in this dataset in any form. Whatever the Watch contributes to a quantified-self app, it will not be screen time.

TWO SILENT PRECONDITIONS WILL BLOCK ENROLLMENT AND THE ERROR NAMES ARE THE ONLY CLUE. FamilyControlsError.authorizationConflict means 'Another authorized app already provides parental controls' - any existing third-party screen-time or app-blocker app on the device will refuse your enrollment until it is revoked or removed, and DeviceActivityAuthorizing.isAuthorized(_ bundleIdentifier:) is the undocumented way to find out which one. FamilyControlsError.authenticationMethodUnavailable means the device has NO PASSCODE SET - individual enrollment requires one, because the Face ID/Touch ID confirmation has nothing to fall back on. Both surface as an opaque throw at first launch and both cost hours if you do not know the enum.

THERE IS NO Info.plist USAGE-DESCRIPTION STRING ANYWHERE IN THIS DOMAIN - WHICH IS EXACTLY WHY IT IS THE HARDEST AREA. Every other iOS telemetry surface (HealthKit, Location, Motion, Contacts, Photos) is gated by a usage-description key plus a runtime prompt, and every one of those works on a free Apple ID. Screen Time is gated by a SIGNED ENTITLEMENT plus a biometric-confirmed system authorization, and the entitlement is withheld from the free tier. That is the entire structural difference: for HealthKit you write a sentence in a plist; for Screen Time you buy a developer account. Anyone budgeting a personal quantified-self app should treat this domain as the one line item that has a price tag on it.

iOS 27 IS IN BETA, NOT SHIPPED, AND BRINGS NOTHING HERE - VERIFIED MECHANICALLY. iOS 27 was announced at WWDC on 8 June 2026, developer beta 3 landed 6 July, public beta is running in July 2026, and general release is expected ~mid-September 2026. iOS 26.5 is the current shipping release. I checked this against Apple's own symbol metadata rather than press coverage: 49 symbols across the crawled documentation carry platform beta flags at 27.0 (Background Inference, private-cloud-compute, media-device-extension, Trust Insights, Suggested Actions, EnergyKit, the macOS ManagedApp providers), and NOT ONE of them is in DeviceActivity, FamilyControls, ManagedSettings or ManagedSettingsUI. The Screen Time story in 2026 is entirely 26.4 and 26.5 - waiting for iOS 27 buys nothing in this domain.
